rag_matches.description: Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Colon, San Bias, Veraguas, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Code (El Valle) and Panama (Cerro Campana), and from tropical wet forest in Code (La Mesa) and Panama.

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Cantarrana, around the station.
Distribution
From Mexico to Brazil. In Costa Rica, widespread in very humid wet forests on both slopes; 0-1,150 m.
Habit
Tree, 10-35 m tall.
Trunk
Cylindrical trunk, with slender, cylindrical, grayish twigs; small stipules attached to the petiole.
Bark
With smooth, grayish bark.
Leaves
Simple, alternate leaves, 2.5-12 x 0.8-5 cm, ovate to oblong, acuminate apex, rounded to cupped base, whitish or grayish on the underside, 5-9 pairs of secondary veins, entire margin; petioles 3-7 mm long.
Flowers
Greenish-yellow flowers, 1.5 mm long, with absent petals and 3-5 stamens. Inflorescences panicles, up to 16 cm long.

Fruits drupes, 1.5-1.8 cm long, pear-shaped to ovoid, pink when ripe.

Distinguished by its clearly bicolored leaves, the underside whitish to grayish and the thin blade with very fine reticulation. Also, by its pear-shaped fruits.

Generally observed in forests on rolling terrain.

Fruits observed in July.

Androdioecious liana or scandent shrub; young stems, petioles, and axes of inflorescences with moderate to dense stellate pubescence interspersed with simple trichomes. Petioles 3-10 mm long, winged full length; blades elliptic to obovate, rounded to abruptly acuminate (rarely short-acuminate), acute to obtuse and decurrent on petiole at base, 5-18 cm long, 3-8 cm wide, the pubescence minute, pustular, stellate on both surfaces, the simple trichomes mostly restricted to veins; lateral veins in 15-25 pairs. Panicles spikelike; flowers unisexual, usually subsessile, 4-5 mm broad, closely congested; sepals 5; petals (2)3(4), pale yellow to greenish-white, rounded at apex, soon falling, the margin folded inward; stamens numerous, to ca 5 mm long, reduced in pistillate flowers; pistils reduced in staminate flowers; style usually directed to one side; stigma ± spatulate-truncate. Follicle 1, glabrous, shiny, dark brown, 5-7 mm long (excluding prominent beak), dehiscing on one side from style downward to expose seed; seeds 1-4, shiny, black, 3-4 mm long, enveloped at least in part by a deeply lacerate red aril. Frequent along the shore and in the forest. Flowering may be induced throughout much of the year, but the chief flowering period is the early dry season (December to March, especially January and February). Flowering appears to be induced by drought. Severing a vine in the proper stage of bud will soon cause the flowers to open. The fruits mature mostly from March to May (sometimes from February). Mexico to Colombia.

Distribution
Nicaragua to southern Brazil, Bolivia, and Peru. In Costa Rica, widespread on both slopes, in humid to very humid climates, 0-1200m?. Common in LS.
Habit
Trees, 10-30 m tall.
Trunk
Straight or sometimes curved at the base, cylindrical, smooth outer bark; red sap; stipules absent.
Bark
Smooth outer bark; red sap.
Leaves
Simple, alternate leaves, 8–25 x 2.7–9 cm, oblong to narrowly oblong-ovate, apex acute to acuminate, base obtuse to truncate or subcordate, with a short pubescence of star-shaped trichomes and glaucous or whitish on the underside, secondary veins 10-28 per side, margin entire; petiole 0.8-2.5 cm long.
Flowers
Staminate inflorescences panicles with many flowers, tepals 3-4, 1.5–3 mm long; anthers 3(-4); pistillate flowers solitary or in clusters of 3-7 cm long; ovary 1-carpellate.
Fruits
Drupe fruit, 10-30 per inflorescence, 1.5–3 x 1-1.7 cm, subglobose to ellipsoid, dehiscent in 2 valves, densely reddish-starry.
Seeds
Subglobose seed, the aril lacerated.
Diagnosis
Recognized by its typical whorled branching, long horizontal branches, distichous leaves, with a truncated or rounded base, the blade with a whitish underside and a pubescence of short star-shaped hairs. Sometimes confused with
V. koschnyi,
but the trees of
V. sebifera
develop lesser height and diameter, the leaves generally have a truncated base, the secondary veins more distant from each other and not forming an evident submarginal vein near the margin, sometimes glaucous on the underside.

Shrub or tree, 3-20(-25) m, the stems ribbed to sub-cylindrical (with age), tomentose to hirsute or hirsute (more sparsely with age) to (sometimes) glabrescent, with few lenticels distributed randomly or (rarely) in short irregular rows. Leaves with petiole 3.3-6.5 cm; petiolules 0.2—1 cm; leaflets 3-11, 6-14.8(-19) X 4.4-11.4(-14.5) cm, [unclear reference], acute to obtuse at the base of the apex, entire.

Tree, 4.5-35 m, the young twigs minutely adpressed-pubescent to glabrescent. Leaves with the petiole 0.5-1.2 cm; blade 10-30 X 3.5-12 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, acute to obtuse or (rarely) subtruncate at the base, glabrous on the underside, without domatia or (rarely) with countable trichomes in the axils of the main veins, with (4)5-8 secondary veins on each side. Inflorescences [of Nectandra purpurea] 10-17 cm. Flowers with the tepals (1—)1.2—2(—2.4) mm. Fruits 1-1.5 cm, ellipsoidal; cup ca. 0.3 cm. Very wet and pluvial forest, 0-1550 m; Caribbean [vertical] Cords. of Guanacaste, Triarán and Central (E.B. La Selva), San Carlos and Tortuguero Plains, Low Talamanca, both [vertical] Cord. de Talamanca, [Pacific] vertical, S Coastal Range (Fila Cruces). Flowers [of Nectandra purpurea] May-Sept. [in Nicaragua, Bolivia] and [Venezuela], [in the] Guiana [region], [in] Brazil. (Grayum et al. 8898, MO) Nectandra purpurea is recognized by its leaf blades that dry relatively opaque on the adaxial side, with the secondary veins slightly elevated and interconnected, forming a submarginal vein and by its flowers with the tepals densely covered by brown or yellowish trichomes and (usually) with the staminodes conspicuously elevated. The cupules that dry light brown, ± puberulent, are also distinctive.

Tree, 3.5-11 (13) m tall; trunk usually 6-15 cm dbh; bark with moderately close, deep vertical fissures, but not flaking; young stems, axes of inflorescences, petioles, and underside of veins densely rufous-pubescent, the trichomes pinnately branched, often somewhat stalked. Petioles to 9 cm long; blades broadly elliptic, obtuse to abruptly short-acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, 9-35 cm long, 6-18 cm wide, denticulate, the surface below canescent and completely covered with trichomes, these sessile, stellate, in part with a brown center; veins 5, dark. Panicles large, terminal, 18-22 cm long, branched many times, the branches ± flattened or angulate; flowers ± sessile; hypanthium and calyx together 1.5-2 mm long, campanulate, the teeth obscure or lacking; petals 5, white, obovate, to 1.5 mm long. Berries round to depressedglobose, to 6 mm diam, white to lavender-blue, probably becoming purple-black at full maturity; seeds numerous, minute. Croat 5693, 15070. Known only from shoreline north of the dock and south of Fairchild Point, but undoubtedly more abundant. Seasonal behavior uncertain. Flowers at least in January, February, and May. Mature fruits have been seen in April, May, and October. Easily confused with Miconia argentea, which is similar in most respects except pubescence, trunk bark, and stature. The species ranges from Mexico to Panama and Venezuela; West Indies. In Panama, the species is known only from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Panama and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone.

Functionally unisexual tree, to 18 m tall, to 27 cm dbh; outer bark thin, flaking in firm sheets, lenticellate; inner bark moderately thick, reddish; sap slowly forming viscid, cloudy droplets after slash, with strong, sweet aroma; stems glabrous, prominently brown-lenticellate. Leaves imparipinnate; petioles flattened above with sharp margins; petiolules thickened at both ends; leaflets 5-9 (13), mostly oblong to oblong-elliptic, acuminate with blunt acumen, acute to rounded at base, often ± inequilateral, 10-20(27) cm long, 5-9(12) cm wide, glabrous except for minute papillae. Panicles axillary, near stem apex, the branches ferruginous; staminate inflorescences somewhat larger than pistillate inflorescences (to 24 cm long); flowers 5-parted, sessile, 3.5-5 mm long; calyx to 2 mm long, cupulate, 5-lobed, minutely pubescent, the lobes acute; petals lanceolate, yellow-green, thickened medially on outside, ca 3 mm long, erect to somewhat spreading at anthesis; stamens 10, alternately long and short, the longest to 2 mm long, the shortest to 1.3 mm long, scarcely longer than the prominent, pubescent disk; ovary ovoid, densely pubescent; style short, the ovary and style together ca 2.7 mm long; stigma 5-lobed, persisting in fruit. Capsules drupaceous, bearing 1-5 pyrenes, ovoid to depressed-globose, with 4 or 5 lobes (rarely 2- or 3-lobed), mostly 2-3 cm diam, red at maturity, usually rounded at both ends, the carpels 4 or 5, each dehiscing by a single valve, the valve falling free to expose the white mesocarp surrounding the pyrene; pyrenes black, 1 per carpel, 1-seeded, ovoid in face view, irregular in side view. Croat 11109, 14822. Common along the shore; occasional in the forest. Flowers chiefly in April and May. The fruits mature chiefly in the middle of the rainy season (August to October). Small bees, possibly Trigona species, have been seen visiting the flowers. The fruits are edible. Costa Rica and Panama. In Panama, known only from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Chiriqui Province, Panama, and Darien Province. Reported from tropical wet forest in Costa Rica (Holdridge et al, 1971).

Polygamous tree, to 35 m high; trunk ca 1 m dbh, buttressed; outer bark with short fissures, thick, irregular on the inner edge; inner bark reddish with white mottling, forming sap droplets; sap yellow, viscid, with the odor of fresh pumpkin; wood white, soft, lightweight; [the subject plant] glabrous except for dense, minute, ferruginous trichomes on young stems and inflorescences. Petioles 2-4 cm long, stout; blades oblong, rounded to emarginate at apex, mostly obtuse at base, 11-20 cm long, 4.5-9.5 cm wide (to 30 cm long and 8.5 cm wide on juvenile [specific specimens]), coriaceous; lateral veins very fine and parallel, secondary lateral veins lacking. Racemes short, to 4.5 cm long; inflorescence branches, petals, and sepals densely ferruginoustomentose; pedicels less than 5 mm long; buds globose; sepals 4, ± orbicular to broadly elliptic, concave, ca 6-8 mm long, yellow, markedly unequal in width on a single flower, the outermost wider, about half as wide as long.

Shrub or tree, 3-20(-25) m, the stems ribbed to sub-cylindrical (with age), tomentose to hirsute or hirsute (more sparsely with age) to (sometimes) glabrescent, with few lenticels distributed randomly or (rarely) in short irregular rows. Leaves with petiole 3.3-6.5 cm; petiolules 0.2—1 cm; leaflets 3-11, 6-14.8(-19) X 4.4-11.4-14.5) cm, [unclear reference], acute to obtuse at the base of the apex, entire.

Locating an individual
Forest, Tree with plate # 926.
Distribution
From Nicaragua to Colombia and Venezuela. In Costa Rica, widespread in very humid climates of the Caribbean slope and the central part to the southwest of the Pacific slope, 0-750 (-1000) m.
Habit
Tree or shrub, 3-10 m tall.
Leaves
Simple leaves, alternate, 3-17 × 1-6 cm, elliptical, elliptic-oblong or oblanceolate, long acuminate apex, attenuated base, glabrous, margin subentire, crenate or serrate.
Flowers
Yellowish or white-greenish flowers; sepals 4, very small; petals absent; stamens 1. Inflorescences racemose, solitary or 2-3 per axil, 4-14 cm long.
Fruits
Fruit capsule, 3-4 mm long, globose, orange when ripe.
Seeds
Seeds 1 (-3), smooth, with a red to orange aril.
Diagnosis
Characterized by its distichous leaves, with finely serrated margin, relatively thin blade, and fine scalariform tertiary venation. When in bloom, distinguished by its slender and pendulous inflorescence.
Habitat
In the Forest; Central Road (CC).
Phenology
